meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Well, every one for himself, and Providence for us all — as the elephant said when he danced among the chickens'?
meta.ogDescription: Wikiquote files it under Dickens's Misattributed heading. The real source: Charles Reade, A Simpleton (1873), chapter 13 — confirmed word for word.

answer.label: Not Charles Dickens — actually Charles Reade
answer.sourceLine: The line is a piece of dialogue from Charles Reade’s novel A Simpleton: A Story of the Day, first published in three volumes by Chapman and Hall in 1873. It is spoken in Chapter XIII by Lieutenant Fitzroy, needling the invalid young Lord Tadcaster over who gets the safer bunk aboard ship — and it appears verbatim in the full text at Project Gutenberg ↗. Wikiquote files it under Charles Dickens’s Misattributed heading and credits Reade.

source.heading: The source, located

docMeta.dd: A Simpleton: A Story of the Day
Chapter XIII — spoken by Lieutenant Fitzroy to Lord Tadcaster
Charles Dickens — listed under “Misattributed” on Wikiquote

source.excerpt:
“He is not ill: I am. He is paid to take care of me: I am not paid to take care of him,” said the young lord sententiously.

“I understand,” replied Fitzroy, dryly. “Well, every one for himself, and Providence for us all—as the elephant said when he danced among the chickens.”
trail: The wording appears verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text of A Simpleton ↗, in Chapter XIII, as Lieutenant Fitzroy’s reply to Lord Tadcaster.
Wikiquote’s Charles Dickens page ↗ places the quotation under Misattributed and credits “Charles Reade, A Simpleton (1873)”; the Charles Reade page ↗ carries it with the same source.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of A Simpleton: A Story of the Day, in Three Volumes ↗, dated 1873 and published by Chapman and Hall of London — independent confirmation of the year.

The pull toward Dickens is easy to explain: this style of joke is a Wellerism ↗, named after Sam Weller in Dickens’s The Pickwick Papers. That is an association, not an attribution — a search of the full Gutenberg text of Pickwick finds no “chickens” and no “Providence for us all”.
source.excerptNote: The two men are aboard ship, dividing up the sleeping berths: Fitzroy has offered the invalid Lord Tadcaster his choice, and the boy has just taken the safe standing bed and left the swinging cot to his doctor.

author.name: Charles Reade
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: Charles Reade (8 June 1814 – 11 April 1884) was a British novelist and dramatist, best remembered today for the historical romance The Cloister and the Hearth (1861). He built his reputation on campaigning fiction — It Is Never Too Late to Mend (1856) attacked prison conditions and Hard Cash (1863) went after private lunatic asylums — though he rated Griffith Gaunt (1866) his own best book. A Simpleton (1873), the novel that carries this line, is one of his later society stories, and its dialogue has the brisk comic snap that keeps getting mistaken for his more famous contemporary.

misattribution.heading: How Dickens got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the cleanest misattributions in the quote world: a real line, from a real Victorian novel, by the wrong Victorian novelist.

items.why: Wikiquote carries the quotation in the Misattributed section of its Charles Dickens page ↗ and credits Charles Reade, A Simpleton (1873). Quote aggregators still headline it as a Dickens line — one page ↗ prints “Charles Dickens” at the top and then flags it as misattributed to Reade directly underneath.

items.who: “Every man for himself, as the elephant said…”
items.why: The version that circulates usually drops Reade’s middle clause, “and Providence for us all”, which is the half the joke is actually deflating. Tommy Douglas’s much-quoted parliamentary version, sourced on Wikiquote ↗ to the Budget Debate in the House of Commons, Ottawa, 22 March 1943, runs “It is the law of every man for himself, as the elephant said when he was dancing among the chickens.”

A HuffPost column ↗ recalls an old cartoon of an elephant cavorting in a chicken coop and describes its caption as a paraphrase of Dickens — a good illustration of how the credit travels without anyone checking a text.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Charles Reade’s, given to Lieutenant Fitzroy in Chapter XIII of A Simpleton (1873) — readable in full at Project Gutenberg ↗.

context.heading: Why this line keeps getting borrowed
lead: Reade’s joke is a Wellerism: a proverb hijacked by a literal-minded speaker who ruins it. The proverbial half — every one for himself, and Providence for us all — sounds like humble resignation until an elephant says it while trampling a coop. The form is named after Sam Weller in Dickens’s The Pickwick Papers, serialised March 1836 to November 1837 and issued as a book in 1837, which is very likely why a Wellerism written by somebody else keeps drifting back onto Dickens’s shelf.

The gag also had a long political afterlife. In the Budget Debate in the House of Commons in Ottawa on 22 March 1943, Tommy Douglas turned it into an argument: free enterprise, he said, is the law of every man for himself, as the elephant said when he was dancing among the chickens — fine if you are in the elephant class, depressing if you are a farmer or a worker in the chicken group.
detailsBody: The wording was matched character-for-character against the Project Gutenberg text of A Simpleton, where it sits in Chapter XIII inside a two-line exchange between Lieutenant Fitzroy and Lord Tadcaster.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of the 1873 Chapman and Hall three-volume first edition, which fixes the publication year independently of the Gutenberg transcription.

We searched the full Gutenberg text of The Pickwick Papers for the phrase. “Chickens” does not occur in the book at all, and neither does “Providence for us all”; the four uses of “elephant” are unrelated.
context.pull: The proverb sounds pious. The elephant makes it a confession.

sourcesVerified.claim: The exact wording "Well, every one for himself, and Providence for us all--as the elephant said when he danced among the chickens" appears in Charles Reade's A Simpleton, in Chapter XIII, spoken by Lieutenant Fitzroy in reply to Lord Tadcaster.

Project Gutenberg's full text of A Simpleton contains the line verbatim; the last chapter heading before it is CHAPTER XIII, and the surrounding dialogue is the berth-choosing exchange between Fitzroy and Lord Tadcaster.
Project Gutenberg hosts a free edition of A Simpleton by Charles Reade (ebook no. 2301).
Wikiquote's Charles Dickens page lists this quotation in its Misattributed section and credits Charles Reade, A Simpleton (1873).
Wikiquote's Charles Reade page carries the quotation with the source A Simpleton (1873).
This quote-aggregator page headlines the line as a Charles Dickens quote and then flags it 'Misattributed', naming Charles Reade, A Simpleton (1873) as the real source.

Charles Reade lived 8 June 1814 to 11 April 1884, was a British novelist and dramatist, and A Simpleton is listed among his works with the publication year 1873; his best-known works include The Cloister and the Hearth (1861), It Is Never Too Late to Mend (1856), Hard Cash (1863) and Griffith Gaunt (1866).
The Internet Archive holds a scan titled 'A Simpleton: A Story of the Day, in Three Volumes, Vol. I' by Charles Reade.
The Internet Archive metadata for that item gives date 1873 and publisher 'Chapman and Hall (London)'.

Wikiquote's Tommy Douglas page sources to the Budget Debate, House of Commons, Ottawa, Ontario, March 22, 1943 the passage: 'It is the law of every man for himself, as the elephant said when he was dancing among the chickens. That is not a bad philosophy if... you happen to be in the elephant class, but it is likely to be depressing if you are a farmer or worker, and belong in the chicken group.'
A HuffPost column recalls a Depression-era cartoon of an elephant cavorting in a chicken coop and says its caption 'paraphrased Dickens'.
Wellerisms are named after the sayings of Sam Weller in Charles Dickens's novel The Pickwick Papers.
The Pickwick Papers was serialised March 1836 to November 1837 and published in book form in 1837.
The full Gutenberg text of The Pickwick Papers contains no occurrence of 'chickens' and no occurrence of 'Providence for us all'; its four uses of 'elephant' are unrelated to this saying.
